title: Five PMs in Seven Years: Is the UK Becoming Ungovernable?
summary: The numbers are staggering: five prime ministers in seven years, none lasting a full parliamentary term. The UK has churned through leaders at a pace once associated with Italy, prompting a pressing question: is the country becoming ungovernable? Prime Minister Keir Starmer and Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch both reject that label, but the turmoil is undeniable. Analysts point to a perfect storm of factors. First, the sheer weight of crises: the 2008 financial crash, the divisive Brexit process, the COVID-19 pandemic, the energy shock from the Ukraine war, and the disruptive return of Donald Trump. These global headwinds have toppled incumbents across Europe. Yet many argue the UK's problems run deeper. Hannah White of the Institute for Government says political parties have elevated prime ministers "lacking in key leadership skills." Historian Sir Anthony Seldon is blunter: recent leaders like Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, and even Starmer lacked the political abilities and humility to seek help. "They didn't have the skills and weren't willing to bring people in," he said. Compounding this is a civil service that some ministers accuse of obstruction, while officials privately blame ministers for unclear instructions. Starmer himself has expressed frustration: "Every time I go to pull a lever, there are a whole bunch of regulations... that mean the action... is longer than I think it ought to be." Then there's social media. Theo Bertram, a former adviser to Tony Blair, notes that fixing a country takes a decade, but "in the age of social media, what you have is a lot of short-termism." WhatsApp groups enable rebellions to organize in days, not months. Former Tory MP Steve Baker observed that "whips and ministers arrive too late to a conversation that social media concluded an hour ago." The result is a political system that feels perpetually on edge, where leaders are disposable and long-term planning is a luxury.
why_it_matters: When a country lurches from one leader to another, long-term challenges like climate change, education, and inequality get sidelined. The way politics works now, shaped by social media and quick rebellions, could mean the problems young people care about are never properly addressed.

keywords.explanation: Ungovernable means a country is so divided or disorganized that it is extremely difficult to run effectively.
Parliamentary relates to a system of government with a parliament—an elected body that makes laws and chooses the prime minister.
Incumbents are people currently holding a political office, such as a prime minister or president.
A civil service is the group of permanent government employees, not elected politicians, who carry out the day-to-day work of running a country.
Short-termism is a focus on quick results and immediate problems rather than long-term planning and solutions.
Whips are party officials in a legislature whose job is to make sure members vote according to the party line and maintain discipline.

background_read: The United Kingdom has a Westminster-style parliamentary system where the prime minister is usually the leader of the largest party in the House of Commons and can be replaced by their own party between elections.
Italy was long known for rapid turnover in governments, with over 60 governments since 1946; the UK's recent instability has drawn comparisons.

The 2008 global financial crisis triggered a recession that damaged public trust, while the 2016 Brexit referendum deeply split the country and contributed to the rapid downfall of multiple prime ministers.
Boris Johnson (Prime Minister 2019–2022) resigned after a series of scandals; Liz Truss (PM for just 45 days in 2022) was brought down by a budget crisis.
Sir Anthony Seldon is a contemporary historian who has written biographies of every recent British prime minister and is often consulted on political leadership.
The Institute for Government is a non-partisan UK think tank that researches how to make government more effective.

perspectives.description: Some argue that replacing underperforming leaders quickly is a sign of a responsive system, not a failing one. A swift change can prevent a prime minister from causing more damage and might open the door for new ideas.

Frequent turnover creates instability that frightens investors, weakens the civil service, and makes it almost impossible to tackle long-term problems. The public may become cynical when leaders are seen as disposable and out of touch.

The UK's turmoil isn't unique; many Western democracies face similar pressures from social media, economic shocks, and polarisation. The pattern suggests a systemic shift as much as a failure of individual leaders.

To escape the cycle of short-termism, reformers propose longer parliamentary terms, better leadership training within parties, and changes to the whipping system. The future may depend on whether politicians can adapt to the speed-of-social-media era without losing the ability to plan ahead.
